newsitem.title: INDIA: India tea trade seeks ways to boost falling exports.
newsitem.headline: India tea trade seeks ways to boost falling exports.

text.p: COONOR, India, Sept 29 (REUTER) - The Indian tea industry needs to win back world market share, otherwise falling exports will weigh on domestic prices, trade sources said at a conference here on Sunday.

"Between now and December domestic tea prices will fall sharply unless India extends long-term credit to Russia to wean that country away from the Sri Lankan teas," Somnath Sen, a director of Contemporary Tea Target, a Calcutta based broker, told Reuters.
Sen was attending the United Planters Association of Southern India (UPASI) annual conference at this picturesque hill resort in the heart of India's southern tea growing region.
"Tea exports have been going down and consequently so has India's share of the world market," UPASI said in a report presented at the start of the two day conference.
"India should regain its share, hence export thrust should get maximum attention," UPASI said.

India's tea exports had fallen sharply to 150,700 tonnes by 1994 from 215,0000 in 1991 and recovered marginally to 163,700 in 1995. The tea industry and trade have set a target of 180,000 tonnes for export in 1996.
The collapse of the Soviet Union, which accounted for nearly 50 percent of its tea exports, is the main reason for the decline in Indian tea exports since 1991.
India's tea industry and trade have had little success in their efforts to sell a special India blend to the Commonwealth for Independent States (CIS), comprising former members of the Soviet Union.
Delegates Sri lanka had entrenched itself in export markets in Russia and other former-Soviet countries by offering easy credit terms to buyers.

Subodh Paul, a colleague of Sen's at Contemporary Tea Target, said that Russia was buying Sri Lankan tea at around 80 rupees per kg against an average Indian offer of around 40 rupees mainly because of favourable credit offered by Sri Lanka.

"There's also the quality difference which is in favour of Sri lankan teas. The shelf life of Indian teas exported to Russia is about nine weeks while that of Sri Lankan teas is about 18 months," Paul said.
Sen said he would expect Indian tea prices to fall because of the total absence of Russia and CIS countries at Indian auctions.
The Russian buyers have been absent at Indian tea auctions since May, June this year.
UPASI said world tea exports had been steadily rising for years but plateaued after 1989 although a record 1.153 million tonnes export shipments was hit in 1993.
In 1995 world export shipments were 1.065 million tonnes in 1995, just up from 1.026 million in 1994.
The UPASI conference will also discuss various issues related to the coffee and rubber plantation industries, and spices, especially pepper and cardamom.
